source.verbatim_note: Text copied exactly from the library file. Lines within each paragraph are joined, and runs of spaces (the filing's double spaces after periods) are collapsed to single spaces. Nothing else is changed, including the original's stray comma in '$371 million, merchant assets'.

intro.text: Every annual report ends with notes that explain the numbers. Note 16 of Enron's report for 2000 is about one page long. It describes deals between Enron and partnerships run by one of its own top executives. The deals were disclosed, at least to some extent, yet almost no reader could tell what was going on. Below, the note appears in full, exactly as Enron filed it. Tap or hover over a highlighted phrase to see what it said in plain English, what it left out, and what the investigations later found.

annotations.phrase: RELATED PARTY TRANSACTIONS
annotations.said: This is Note 16 of the notes attached to Enron's financial statements for 2000. Enron's Form 10-K, the annual report a public company files with the SEC, was signed on March 30, 2001. A related party transaction is a deal between a company and someone closely tied to it, such as one of its own officers. The rules require such deals to be disclosed because the usual assumption, that each side bargains hard for itself, may not hold.
annotations.left_out: The heading promises an explanation of Enron's deals with insiders. The note that follows never names the partnerships, the officer, or the entities involved. It also never gives the bottom line: how much of Enron's profit these deals produced.
annotations.found: The board's special committee (the Powers Committee) found that Enron "failed to disclose facts that were important for an understanding of the substance of the transactions." The Senate subcommittee staff found the 2000 footnote "nearly unintelligible." Sherron Watkins wrote to Enron's board chairman, Kenneth Lay, in August 2001 that "the footnotes don't adequately explain the transactions," as quoted in the staff report. The bankruptcy examiner concluded that Enron "failed to make appropriate disclosures of its SPE transactions to the public."

paragraphs.text: In 2000 and 1999, Enron entered into transactions with limited partnerships (the Related Party) whose general partner's managing member is a senior officer of Enron. The limited partners of the Related Party are unrelated to Enron. Management believes that the terms of the transactions with the Related Party were reasonable compared to those which could have been negotiated with unrelated third parties.

annotations.phrase: Enron entered into transactions with limited partnerships (the Related Party)
annotations.said: In 1999 and 2000, Enron did business with some limited partnerships and grouped them under one label, "the Related Party." A limited partnership is a kind of investment fund. A general partner runs it, and limited partners put in money.
annotations.left_out: The partnerships were LJM Cayman, L.P. ("LJM1") and LJM2 Co-Investment, L.P. ("LJM2"). Enron had named them in earlier filings. From mid-2000 on, the financial statements used only the generic label.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found: "From the second quarter of 2000 forward, Enron did not identify LJM1 or LJM2 by name in the financial statement disclosures." After the collapse began, Enron disclosed in November 2001 that there had been 24 business relationships with LJM1 or LJM2 between June 1999 and September 2001.

cites.loc: Powers Report, p. 193, VIII.D.1 Enron's Disclosures (lines 6906ff. of SEC text)
cites.quote: From the second quarter of 2000 forward, Enron did not identify LJM1 or LJM2 by name in the financial statement disclosures, using the generic term "Related Party" instead.

cites.loc: Enron Form 8-K, Nov. 8, 2001, p. 10, B. General Summary of LJM Transactions (line 469)
cites.quote: From June 1999 through September 2001, Enron and Enron-related entities entered into 24 business relationships in which LJM1 or LJM2 participated.

annotations.phrase: whose general partner's managing member is a senior officer of Enron
annotations.said: The person in charge of the partnerships was a top Enron executive.
annotations.left_out: The officer was Andrew Fastow, Enron's Chief Financial Officer (CFO), the executive responsible for its finances. The same 10-K lists Fastow as CFO in another section, but this note never connects the two. It also says nothing about what he earned from the partnerships. (Enron's proxy statement, a different document sent to shareholders, did name Fastow as managing member of LJM1's general partner.)
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the footnote "did not identify Fastow" in this or any later financial statement. It found that Fastow was enriched "by at least $30 million" and that he "did not want his compensation from the LJM partnerships to be disclosed." In November 2001, Enron disclosed that it "now believes that Mr. Fastow received in excess of $30 million." The Senate subcommittee staff found that a year after the board's Finance Committee asked for information on Fastow's LJM pay, no board member had obtained it.

annotations.phrase: The limited partners of the Related Party are unrelated to Enron.
annotations.said: The note says the investors in the partnerships had no ties to Enron.
annotations.left_out: Several Enron employees secretly held financial stakes connected to the partnerships. Michael Kopper, an Enron employee who reported to Fastow, held an interest in LJM2's general partner through an entity called Big Doe. In March 2000, a partnership called Southampton Place was set up to buy part of an existing LJM1 limited partner's interest. Its investors included Fastow's family foundation, Kopper, Ben Glisan (who became Enron's Treasurer in May 2000), and other employees.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that this happened "Unbeknownst to virtually everyone at Enron." It found that the Fastow family foundation turned a $25,000 investment into $4.5 million in about two months. The SEC alleged the same payout in its complaint against Fastow. By November 2001, Enron's own wording had softened to say the partnerships had "a significant number of" limited partners that were not related parties.

annotations.phrase: Management believes that the terms of the transactions with the Related Party were reasonable compared to those which could have been negotiated with unrelated third parties.
annotations.said: Enron's managers said the deals were about as good as deals with outsiders would have been. This is the claim that the deals were made "at arm's length," between independent parties.
annotations.left_out: The note does not show any evidence for the claim. It also does not show that the wording had been weakened from one filing to the next. In 1999, Enron said the terms were "reasonable and no less favorable" than outside deals. In 2000, it said only that they were "reasonable compared to" what could have been negotiated.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Enron "lacked the factual basis required by the accounting literature" for this sentence. It noted that drafts had handwritten notes reading "need positive evidence." It found that "many of them could only have been entered into with related parties." The committee also found that Andersen, Enron's auditor, told the board's Audit and Compliance Committee that the required disclosure had been "reviewed for adequacy."

paragraphs.text: In 2000, Enron entered into transactions with the Related Party to hedge certain merchant investments and other assets. As part of the transactions, Enron (i) contributed to newly-formed entities (the Entities) assets valued at approximately $1.2 billion, including $150 million in Enron notes payable, 3.7 million restricted shares of outstanding Enron common stock and the right to receive up to 18.0 million shares of outstanding Enron common stock in March 2003 (subject to certain conditions) and (ii) transferred to the Entities assets valued at approximately $309 million, including a $50 million note payable and an investment in an entity that indirectly holds warrants convertible into common stock of an Enron equity method investee. In return, Enron received economic interests in the Entities, $309 million in notes receivable, of which $259 million is recorded at Enron's carryover basis of zero, and a special distribution from the Entities in the form of $1.2 billion in notes receivable, subject to changes in the principal for amounts payable by Enron in connection with the execution of additional derivative instruments. Cash in these Entities of $172.6 million is invested in Enron demand notes. In addition, Enron paid $123 million to purchase share-settled options from the Entities on 21.7 million shares of Enron common stock. The Entities paid Enron $10.7 million to terminate the share-settled options on 14.6 million shares of Enron common stock outstanding. In late 2000, Enron entered into share-settled collar arrangements with the Entities on 15.4 million shares of Enron common stock. Such arrangements will be accounted for as equity transactions when settled.

annotations.phrase: to hedge certain merchant investments and other assets
annotations.said: Enron says these deals were hedges, a kind of protection against losses. The losses in question were on its "merchant investments," stakes in other companies that Enron valued at market price every quarter. Under mark-to-market accounting, any drop in those prices reduced Enron's reported profit.
annotations.left_out: A normal hedge moves risk to an outside party that can pay if the loss happens. The note does not say that the party on the other side was built mainly out of Enron's own assets.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that "Enron still bore virtually all of the economic risk. In effect, Enron was hedging risk with itself." The bankruptcy examiner concluded that these were accounting hedges "with the sole purpose of providing financial statement benefits." Vince Kaminski, head of Enron's research group, compared them in a sworn statement to the examiner's staff to buying house insurance from your own spouse: "there's no effective risk transfer to a third party."

cites.loc: Powers Report, p. 97, V. The Raptors (lines 3611ff. of SEC text)
cites.quote: Enron still bore virtually all of the economic risk. In effect, Enron was hedging risk with itself.

cites.loc: Batson Final Report, printed p. 10, Summary of Conclusions, footnote 17
cites.quote: they were accounting hedges (with the sole purpose of providing financial statement benefits) and did not provide economic protection to Enron because the assets used to support the hedge were Enron's own assets

cites.loc: Batson Final Report, printed p. 19, footnote 41 (Kaminski sworn statement)
cites.quote: there's no effective risk transfer to a third party

annotations.phrase: contributed to newly-formed entities (the Entities)
annotations.said: Enron put assets into brand-new companies created for these deals. The note calls them "the Entities."
annotations.left_out: The Entities were four special purpose entities (SPEs) known inside Enron as the Raptors. Their legal names were Talon, Timberwolf, Bobcat and Porcupine. LJM2 put in a small amount of outside money ($30 million in Raptor I, for example) so that Enron could keep the Entities off its own balance sheet. One of them, Raptor III, never went to Enron's board.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Enron referred to the Raptor vehicles as the "Entities" in this footnote. It found that Raptor III "was not presented to the Board or to any of its Committees." In Raptor I, the SEC alleged, an undisclosed side deal promised LJM2 its money back plus a profit before any hedging began. If so, the outside money was never truly at risk, and the SPE should have been counted as part of Enron.

annotations.phrase: $150 million in Enron notes payable, 3.7 million restricted shares of outstanding Enron common stock and the right to receive up to 18.0 million shares of outstanding Enron common stock in March 2003 (subject to certain conditions)
annotations.said: This lists what Enron gave the Entities: IOUs from Enron, Enron shares that could not be sold for a time, and contracts to receive up to 18 million more Enron shares in 2003.
annotations.left_out: Almost everything Enron put in was its own stock or its own promise to pay. The Entities could "pay" Enron on the hedges only while Enron's stock price stayed high. The 18 million shares depended on Enron's stock price on March 1, 2003: below certain levels, some Raptors would receive no shares at all.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the Raptors were "funded principally with Enron's own stock (or contracts for the delivery of Enron stock)." It found that the hedges would work "as long as Enron's stock price remained strong." In her August 2001 letter to Lay, as quoted by the Senate subcommittee staff, Watkins wrote that the "Entities" in the footnote were "thinly capitalized, the equity holders have no skin in the game."

annotations.left_out: The company was The New Power Company (TNPC), which Enron had created and owned 75% of. This piece funded Raptor III, which was meant to hedge Enron's TNPC investment using TNPC itself.
annotations.found: In November 2001, Enron disclosed that "Raptor III was capitalized with an economic interest in warrants convertible into stock of NPW" (New Power). The board's special committee found that Raptor III "held the stock of the very company whose stock it was intended to hedge." It called the arrangement "the derivatives equivalent of doubling-down on a bet on TNPC."

annotations.phrase: $309 million in notes receivable, of which $259 million is recorded at Enron's carryover basis of zero
annotations.said: Enron received $309 million in IOUs. It kept $259 million of that on its books at zero, because the asset it gave up had been carried on its books at zero.
annotations.left_out: The $259 million IOU came from Porcupine, the Raptor III entity, in exchange for TNPC stock. Enron priced that stock at $10.75 a share. Five days earlier, it had told employees the expected public offering price was $18 to $20.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Enron "received a note from Porcupine for $259 million, which Enron recorded at zero." It found that Enron did not obtain a fairness opinion, an outside expert's view on whether the price was fair. It noted that five days earlier, Enron had told employees that the expected price range was "$18.00 to $20.00 per share."

annotations.phrase: a special distribution from the Entities in the form of $1.2 billion in notes receivable
annotations.said: The note says Enron received another $1.2 billion in IOUs from the Entities.
annotations.left_out: The note does not say how these IOUs were recorded, or that the Entities could repay them mainly out of the Enron stock Enron had given them.
annotations.found: The investigations do not tie this exact $1.2 billion figure to one transaction. The board's special committee did find a related error. Enron had recorded the $172 million note it received for Enron shares sold to Talon (Raptor I) as an increase to "notes receivable" and to shareholders' equity, the owners' stake shown on the balance sheet. Andersen and Enron later concluded that this was wrong, and it was corrected in 2001. (This is separate from the $1.2 billion cut to shareholders' equity that Enron announced in October 2001.)

annotations.left_out: Even the Entities' cash was a claim on Enron. If Enron ran into trouble, this cash would not be an independent cushion.
annotations.found: Watkins made a related point about the whole structure in her August 2001 letter, as quoted by the Senate subcommittee staff. She wrote that "all the value in the entities comes from the underlying value of the derivatives" and from "Enron stock and N/P." (N/P is standard shorthand for notes payable, meaning Enron's IOUs. The explanation is ours.)

annotations.phrase: Enron paid $123 million to purchase share-settled options from the Entities on 21.7 million shares of Enron common stock
annotations.said: Enron paid the Entities $123 million for options on its own shares.
annotations.left_out: These were put options, contracts that pay off if a stock falls. In effect, Enron was betting that its own stock would drop. Their real purpose was to send cash to LJM2. In each of three Raptors, Enron paid a $41 million premium. Three times $41 million is $123 million, though that arithmetic is ours: the committee does not say these are the same payments. The money went to LJM2 before any hedging began.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the note did not disclose "that Enron purchased puts on Enron stock". It found that the deal was "on its face, predicated on the assumption that its stock price would decline substantially." It also found that LJM2 reported a 193% annualized return on Raptor I. The SEC alleged there was "no true business purpose for the put option other than to generate funds to pay LJM2."

annotations.phrase: The Entities paid Enron $10.7 million to terminate the share-settled options
annotations.said: The options were ended early, and the Entities paid Enron $10.7 million to cancel them.

annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Talon "returned $4 million of the $41 million option premium to Enron, but nevertheless paid LJM2 $41 million." It found that Raptors II and IV followed the same pattern. The committee's report does not break down the $10.7 million total, so we cannot match it to specific payments.

annotations.phrase: share-settled collar arrangements with the Entities on 15.4 million shares of Enron common stock. Such arrangements will be accounted for as equity transactions when settled.
annotations.said: Enron put "collars" on its own shares held by the Entities. If Enron's stock fell below a floor, Enron would make up the difference. If it rose above a ceiling, the Entities would pay Enron. Because these deals involved Enron's own stock, they were booked as equity transactions and did not pass through profit and loss.
annotations.left_out: The collars were added because Enron's falling stock price was shrinking the Entities' ability to pay Enron. They also undercut the reason the shares had been valued at a discount in the first place: the shares were supposed to be restricted. Board members later said they had not been told about the first collar.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the October 30, 2000 collar for Raptor I (floor $81, ceiling $116) "protected Talon's credit capacity against possible future declines in Enron stock." It found that the collars "effectively lifted the restriction" that had justified the discount. Board members told the Senate subcommittee staff that they had not been told about the October 2000 "collar."

paragraphs.text: In 2000, Enron entered into derivative transactions with the Entities with a combined notional amount of approximately $2.1 billion to hedge certain merchant investments and other assets. Enron's notes receivable balance was reduced by $36 million as a result of premiums owed on derivative transactions. Enron recognized revenues of approximately $500 million related to the subsequent change in the market value of these derivatives, which offset market value changes of certain merchant investments and price risk management activities. In addition, Enron recognized $44.5 million and $14.1 million of interest income and interest expense, respectively, on the notes receivable from and payable to the Entities.

annotations.phrase: derivative transactions with the Entities with a combined notional amount of approximately $2.1 billion
annotations.said: Enron signed derivative contracts with the Entities covering about $2.1 billion of investments. A derivative is a contract whose value depends on something else, such as a stock price. The "notional amount" is the size of the investments the contracts refer to. It is not money that changed hands.
annotations.left_out: The note does not compare this $2.1 billion with what the Entities actually had available to pay Enron.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that by November 2000, the derivatives with Raptors I, II and III had "a notional value of over $1.5 billion." In November 2001, Enron disclosed a notional amount of "approximately $1.9 billion." The three figures cover different periods and groupings, and the sources do not reconcile them.

cites.quote: By November 2000, Enron had entered into derivative transactions with Raptors I, II and III with a notional value of over $1.5 billion.

cites.quote: hedge Enron's risk in certain investments having an aggregate notional amount of approximately $1.9 billion.

annotations.phrase: Enron recognized revenues of approximately $500 million related to the subsequent change in the market value of these derivatives
annotations.said: Enron counted about $500 million of revenue from gains on these contracts.
annotations.left_out: The note does not say how much of Enron's total profit came from these deals.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Raptor "earnings" were more than 80% of Enron's reported pre-tax earnings for the last two quarters of 2000. From the third quarter of 2000 through the third quarter of 2001, the Raptors let Enron avoid reporting "almost $1 billion in losses." Without them, pre-tax earnings for that period would have been $429 million instead of $1.5 billion, a decline of 72%. The bankruptcy examiner concluded that virtually all of Enron's $979 million of 2000 net income came from six accounting techniques, including these hedges.

annotations.said: The gains on the contracts cancelled out losses on Enron's investments, so the losses did not reduce profit.
annotations.left_out: The gains counted only if the Entities could actually pay Enron. By the end of 2000, two of them could not. The note does not mention the problem or the stopgap Enron used to avoid recording a loss.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that by mid-December 2000, Raptors I and III had negative "credit capacity." Enron pooled all four Raptors under a 45-day cross-guarantee dated December 22, 2000, and "did not record a reserve for the year ending December 31, 2000." The committee saw "no evidence that Enron's Board was informed." The hedges failed in 2001, and on October 16, 2001, Enron announced a $544 million after-tax charge.

paragraphs.text: In 1999, Enron entered into a series of transactions involving a third party and the Related Party. The effect of the transactions was (i) Enron and the third party amended certain forward contracts to purchase shares of Enron common stock, resulting in Enron having forward contracts to purchase Enron common shares at the market price on that day, (ii) the Related Party received 6.8 million shares of Enron common stock subject to certain restrictions and (iii) Enron received a note receivable, which was repaid in December 1999, and certain financial instruments hedging an investment held by Enron. Enron recorded the assets received and equity issued at estimated fair value. In connection with the transactions, the Related Party agreed that the senior officer of Enron would have no pecuniary interest in such Enron common shares and would be restricted from voting on matters related to such shares. In 2000, Enron and the Related Party entered into an agreement to terminate certain financial instruments that had been entered into during 1999. In connection with this agreement, Enron received approximately 3.1 million shares of Enron common stock held by the Related Party. A put option, which was originally entered into in the first quarter of 2000 and gave the Related Party the right to sell shares of Enron common stock to Enron at a strike price of $71.31 per share, was terminated under this agreement. In return, Enron paid approximately $26.8 million to the Related Party.

annotations.phrase: In 1999, Enron entered into a series of transactions involving a third party and the Related Party.
annotations.said: In 1999, Enron made a set of linked deals with an outside company and with the Related Party.
annotations.left_out: This was the "Rhythms" deal. Enron had invested $10 million in Rhythms NetConnections, an internet company, and the stake had grown to about $300 million. Enron was not allowed to sell it yet. The Related Party here was LJM1, working through an SPE called LJM Swap Sub. The "third party" was an investment bank that held contracts on Enron shares with Enron.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that Rhythms "was the first time that Enron transferred its own stock to an SPE and used the SPE to 'hedge' an Enron merchant investment". It found that the board approved the deal at the same time it approved Fastow's role in LJM1. The Senate subcommittee staff found that the board approved it "with little study or debate" at a meeting that lasted one hour.

annotations.left_out: The purpose was to put to use the rise in value of Enron's own shares under those contracts. Accounting rules do not let a company count that kind of rise as income.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that "a company is generally precluded from recognizing an increase in value of its own stock" as income. It found that Enron "sought to use what it viewed as this 'trapped' or 'embedded' value."

annotations.left_out: The note does not give their value, the discount, or what LJM1 paid.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the shares were worth about $276 million at market. They were discounted by about 39% because of the restrictions, and LJM1 gave Enron a $64 million note in exchange. The committee counts 3.4 million shares, while the 10-K says 6.8 million. The committee labels its later share counts "post-split," and the board meeting that approved the deal also took up resolutions authorizing a stock split. The 10-K therefore probably uses the post-split number. No library source states the split ratio.

It restated, cutting 1999 net income by $95 million.

annotations.said: To end the Rhythms arrangements, Enron paid the Related Party about $26.8 million.

annotations.found: The sources give different payment figures. The board's special committee found that the price was based on a $30 million proposal from Fastow, that Enron paid a net $16.7 million after offsets, and that Swap Sub received "approximately $27 million cash." The committee found that the value Enron gave up exceeded what it got back "by more than $70 million." It found no fairness opinion and no evidence that the board was told. The SEC alleged that the $30 million price rested on Fastow's "false representation" about what the banks had agreed to take. According to the SEC, NatWest received only $1 million, and much of the rest went to Fastow, Kopper, some bankers, and Southampton investors.

paragraphs.text: In 2000, Enron sold a portion of its dark fiber inventory to the Related Party in exchange for $30 million cash and a $70 million note receivable that was subsequently repaid. Enron recognized gross margin of $67 million on the sale.

annotations.phrase: In 2000, Enron sold a portion of its dark fiber inventory to the Related Party in exchange for $30 million cash and a $70 million note receivable that was subsequently repaid.
annotations.said: "Dark fiber" is fiber-optic cable that has been laid but not yet switched on. Enron sold some to the Related Party for $100 million: $30 million in cash and a $70 million IOU that was later repaid.
annotations.left_out: The buyer was LJM2, on June 30, 2000, the last day of the quarter. The note does not say where the repayment came from. In December 2000, LJM2 sold the remaining fiber to another SPE and used part of the proceeds to repay Enron. At that point, Enron took on a new exposure: a derivative that supported some of that SPE's lenders.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that "There was substantial pressure to close the transaction so that EBS could meet its second quarter numbers." (EBS was Enron Broadband Services.) It found that Fastow, negotiating for LJM2, pressed Enron's own team for better terms. It called this "the fundamental dilemma of the Company's CFO serving concurrently as the managing partner." In November 2001, Enron disclosed that the $70 million credit exposure "was replaced with $61 million in remaining exposure under the derivative contract."

paragraphs.text: In 2000, the Related Party acquired, through securitizations, approximately $35 million of merchant investments from Enron. In addition, Enron and the Related Party formed partnerships in which Enron contributed cash and assets and the Related Party contributed $17.5 million in cash. Subsequently, Enron sold a portion of its interests in the partnerships through securitizations. See Note 3. Also, Enron contributed a put option to a trust in which the Related Party and Whitewing hold equity and debt interests. At December 31, 2000, the fair value of the put option was a $36 million loss to Enron.

annotations.left_out: The note does not say which investments were sold, or that Enron later bought many of them back.
annotations.found: The board's special committee found that the assets "were not specifically identified in the disclosures" and that Enron had a policy against naming counterparties. It wrote: "Even after months of investigation, and with access to Enron's information, we remain uncertain as to what transactions some of the disclosures refer." In November 2001, Enron disclosed that in six of nine SPE investments by LJM, "Enron repurchased all or a portion." The committee found that the footnotes "failed to mention that Enron repurchased some of these assets."

annotations.said: Enron says its profit on these 1999 sales was about $16 million before taxes.
annotations.left_out: "Gains" on sales are only part of the picture. Some sales changed how Enron accounted for related contracts, which produced other income that the gain figure does not include.
annotations.found: In November 2001, Enron disclosed a $16 million gain in 1999 on selling LJM2 a stake in a Polish power project. Enron bought part of that stake back in March 2000, and Whitewing bought the rest. (The amounts match, but no source says this is the same $16 million.) The board's special committee found that the Cuiaba sale "enabled Enron to realize $34 million of mark-to-market income" in the third quarter of 1999. It also found that Fastow told the Finance Committee that the LJM deals generated "earnings" of $229 million in the second half of 1999, a figure the committee could not confirm.

closing.text: Two investigations looked back at this note. The board's special committee found that the related-party deals were disclosed "to some extent." It also found that the note did not let a reader "understand what was going on." After the scandal broke, Enron described the same dealings again in its filings of November 2001. The Senate subcommittee staff contrasted that later version with the 2000 footnote and found that it showed "Enron was quite capable of meaningful public disclosure when motivated."

cites.loc: Senate PSI staff report, printed p. 48, Finding (4), Inadequate Public Disclosure
cites.quote: The 10-Q filing demonstrates that Enron was quite capable of meaningful public disclosure when motivated.

closing.ask_why: Every sentence in Note 16 may have been accurate, yet readers still could not see what was happening. Is a disclosure honest if it is accurate but nobody can understand it? Who should be responsible for making it understandable: the company, its auditors, its lawyers, or its board?
